presenter: Thank you for joining us. This paper examines how changing Confucian and traditionalist orientations in Taiwan are related to the ebbs and flows of the diffuse regime support. The empirical setting is the Asian Barometer Survey Taiwan series, which gives us six waves of data from 2001 to 2022. - first explain why traditionalism may matter for regime support in Taiwan. - why the paper does not treat traditionalism as one general scale. Instead, we move from individual survey items to three dimensions, and from those dimensions to an eight-type typology. - The main empirical question: whether those types help explain establishment support and direct regime support after accounting for political evaluations, election-related variables and socio-demographic controls. [Sources] - NSTC/Conference_info.md - NSTC/MHH-FULL/NSTC-ABS/Traditionalism and Diffuse Regime Support_20260712.docx

presenter: Brief notes: - Begin with the legitimacy puzzle. - Standard explanations: performance, corruption, democratic satisfaction, winner-loser status. - Contribution: ask whether cultural orientations retain explanatory power after these controls. The starting point: the study of political support. We already have strong explanations for why citizens support or distrust political regimes. People respond to economic performance, corruption, satisfaction with democratic practice, partisan attachment and whether their preferred side wins or loses elections. These are all within the literature of retrospective voting and consist a large part of the democratic accountability. epistemic orientations This paper adds a cultural question to that discussion. Taiwan has experienced democratisation, alternation in power and major social change, but older cultural orientations have not simply disappeared and most of the traditional Chinese/Confucian traditions has been preserved. We ask whether attitudes toward authority, hierarchy and social harmony still help explain diffuse support for the establishment and for the system of government. The claim is modest: culture is not the only explanation, but it may structure support in ways that remain visible after the usual political and performance variables are included. [Sources] - Manuscript, Introduction - Easton 1975; Norris 1999, 2011; Anderson et al. 2005; Huang 2016

presenter: Brief notes: - State the core argument in plain terms. - Traditionalism changes through recombination, not only decline. - Three dimensions: Core, Social and General Traditionalism. - Political effect depends on the combination of dimensions. The core argument is that Taiwan's cultural change is better understood as "recombination than as a simple decline of tradition". “Traditional vs. Secular-Rational Values” and “Survival vs. Self-Expression Values”, Some citizens may retain family-centred obligations but reject wider social hierarchy. Others may retain conflict avoidance without accepting stronger authority relations. These are different cultural profiles, and they should not be averaged away. For this reason, the paper separates traditionalism into three dimensions. Core Traditionalism refers to family and Heaven-centred authority. Social Traditionalism refers to wider hierarchical relations, especially in extended-family and teacher-student settings. General Traditionalism refers to conflict avoidance and harmony. The empirical expectation is that support for the establishment and the regime will depend on how these dimensions are combined. [Sources] - Manuscript, Abstract and Theory and Conceptualization

presenter: Brief notes: - Define the three dimensions clearly. - Core: filial obligation and fatalism. - Social: mother-in-law obedience and teacher authority. - General: conflict avoidance. - Explain why collectivism and immediate interest are excluded from the typology. [Differential Mode of Association] of Chinese epistemic orientations [concentric circles] The typology begins with a conceptual distinction inside Confucian and traditionalist orientations. Core Traditionalism combines filial obligation and fatalism. These items locate authority close to the moral centre of the Confucian order: parents and Heaven. Social Traditionalism extends the same logic into wider interpersonal hierarchy. It combines obedience in the mother-in-law relationship with deference to teacher authority. General Traditionalism is measured through conflict avoidance. This item does not name a single authority figure, but it captures the broader norm of accommodation and harmony. The remaining items are not discarded, but they are not used to define the typology. Collectivism is too general because family-centred obligation appears across many civilisational traditions. Immediate interest is closer to interpersonal distance and long-term relationship orientation than to authority or harmony. [Sources] - Manuscript, Theory and Conceptualization - Table 1

presenter: Brief notes: - Data: six ABS Taiwan waves, 2001-2022. - Main outcome: establishment support from trust in people who run government. - Validation outcomes: four direct DRS items in Waves 3-6. - Models: weighted ordered logits with political and demographic controls. The empirical analysis uses six waves of the Asian Barometer Survey in Taiwan, covering the period from 2001 to 2022. The harmonised working file contains 9,042 cases and a common set of traditionalism, political and demographic variables. The main outcome is based on the item asking whether people can generally trust the people who run government to do what is right. We recode this as establishment support so that higher values indicate stronger support. From Wave 3 onward, the ABS also includes direct regime-support questions about the system of government. Those items allow us to check whether the typology predicts system-level support, not only trust in governing elites. All models are weighted ordered-logit models. The controls include winner status, nonpartisanship, unification-independence position, economic evaluation, presidential satisfaction, democratic satisfaction, gender, education, income, subjective status and wave dummies. [Sources] - Manuscript, Data, Measurement and Research Design - All.sps; sup_est.sps

presenter: Brief notes: - This is the measurement bridge between theory and models. - Core: parents and Heaven. - Social: teacher and mother-in-law. - General: conflict avoidance. - Collectivism and immediate interest are not part of the typology. This table is the key measurement step in the paper. The ABS gives us seven long-standing items, but the manuscript does not treat them as a single undifferentiated traditionalism scale. The first two items form Core Traditionalism: obedience to parents and fatalism, or the authority of Heaven. The next two form Social Traditionalism: deference to teachers and obedience in the mother-in-law relationship. The conflict-avoidance item forms General Traditionalism because it captures harmony and accommodation without naming a single authority figure. The final two items are kept in the empirical analysis, but they are not part of the typology. Collectivism is broader than Confucian authority, and immediate interest is closer to interpersonal distance than hierarchy or harmony. This distinction is what allows the next slides to ask which dimensions, and which combinations, matter for regime support. [Sources] - /Users/osbern/Library/CloudStorage/OneDrive-GriffithUniversity/GRANTS/SGIR_RSS_R12026/NSTC/MHH-FULL/NSTC-ABS/Traditionalism and Diffuse Regime Support_20260712.docx, Table 1 and Theory and Conceptualization - /Users/osbern/Library/CloudStorage/OneDrive-GriffithUniversity/GRANTS/SGIR_RSS_R12026/NSTC/MHH-FULL/NSTC-ABS/All.sps

presenter: Brief notes: - Table 2 gives the first empirical clue. - Authority and harmony items are consistently positive. - Teacher authority has the largest item-level association. - Collectivism and immediate interest do not behave like the core authority items. The item-level models provide the first reason to move beyond a single scale. If all traditionalism items behaved in the same way, a general index might be enough. The results do not support that approach. Filial piety, conflict avoidance, fatalism, mother-in-law obedience and teacher authority are positively associated with establishment support. Teacher authority is especially strong in the item-level models. By contrast, collectivism is not associated with support, and immediate interest is weak and unstable. This pattern tells us that the politically relevant content is not tradition in the broadest possible sense. The stronger signal comes from attitudes linked to authority, hierarchy and harmony. That evidence motivates the three-dimensional typology used in the rest of the analysis. [Sources] - Manuscript, Item-Level Empirical Findings - Table 2

presenter: Brief notes: - Present the typology as the main measurement move. - Explain why an additive scale would hide meaningful profiles. - Give examples: Core-only, General-only, fully traditional. - Set up the next slide with the eight combinations. The typology is the main measurement move in the paper. A scale would tell us whether a respondent is more or less traditional overall, but it would hide the configuration of values underneath that score. For example, a respondent can be high on Core Traditionalism while low on Social and General Traditionalism. Another respondent can retain conflict avoidance while rejecting the authority items. A third can score high on all three dimensions. These profiles are not equivalent, even if an additive index might place some of them close together. The typology allows us to ask a more precise question: which combinations of authority and harmony are politically consequential? [Sources] - Manuscript, From Items to Types

presenter: Brief notes: - Explain the shorthand: Core-Social-General. - The slide is about combinations, not just prevalence. - NNY is the largest average type. - YYY remains substantial. - Core-only YNN is small. - NNN becomes the reference group in the models. This slide reports the eight traditionalism types used in the models. The shorthand order is Core, Social and General. Y means high on that dimension, and N means low. The distribution is already part of the argument. The largest average group is Type 5, NNY, meaning respondents who retain conflict avoidance but are not high on Core or Social authority. At the same time, the fully traditional type, YYY, remains substantial at 18 percent. Taiwan's cultural change therefore cannot be described as the disappearance of traditionalism. The small Core-only type is also useful. Only 4.4 percent of respondents are high on Core Traditionalism alone. This prepares the ground for the model results, where Core-only is not the strongest profile. The important move is from a simple traditional-modern continuum to combinations of authority and harmony. [Sources] - Manuscript, Table 3

presenter: Brief notes: - Explain the coefficient plot: reference is NNN. - Six of seven contrasts are positive and significant. - YYY is the strongest association. - Social Traditionalism is important even as Social-only. - Core-only is the exception. This figure summarises the main typology model. The reference group is Type 1, NNN, respondents who are low on all three dimensions. The broad pattern is positive. Six of the seven contrasts are associated with higher establishment support. The largest coefficient belongs to Type 4, YYY, the fully traditional type. Type 3, which combines Core and Social Traditionalism, is also very strong. The Social dimension deserves attention. Type 8, the Social-only group, is positive and significant even though it is low on Core and General Traditionalism. Type 6, Social plus General, is also positive. This suggests that wider social hierarchy is one of the more politically salient parts of the traditionalist structure. The main exception is Type 2, Core-only, which is not statistically distinguishable from the reference group. [Sources] - Manuscript, Typology and Establishment Support - NSTC/MHH-FULL/NSTC-ABS/Figures/Table4_Traditionalism_Types_Establishment_Support_Coefplot.png

presenter: Brief notes: - Use this as the numerical version of the coefficient plot. - NNN is the reference group. - YYY and YYN have the largest estimates. - Social-containing types remain strong. - Core-only remains statistically weak. This table gives the key numerical contrasts from the full establishment-support model. The reference group is NNN, respondents who are low on Core, Social and General Traditionalism. The strongest profile is the fully traditional type, YYY, with a coefficient of .84. The Core plus Social type, YYN, follows closely at .79. These two estimates show that configurations containing authority relations are strongly associated with establishment support. The rest of the table clarifies the role of each dimension. Types that contain Social Traditionalism are consistently positive. General Traditionalism is also positive on its own, but the estimate is smaller. The weakest contrast is Core-only: filial obligation and fatalism matter in the item models, but without Social hierarchy or General harmony, the Core-only type is not statistically distinct from the low-on-all group. [Sources] - Manuscript, Typology and Establishment Support - NSTC/MHH-FULL/NSTC-ABS/Figures/Table4_Traditionalism_Types_Establishment_Support_Coefplot.png

presenter: Brief notes: - Move from pooled models to cultural change over time. - Largest decline: mother-in-law obedience. - Teacher authority also declines. - Conflict avoidance remains high. - Fatalism is stable; filial piety fluctuates. The pooled models show that the typology is associated with support, but they do not show how traditionalist orientations changed over time. The six-wave ABS series allows us to describe that change. The clearest decline is in Social Traditionalism. Obedience in the mother-in-law relationship falls sharply between the first and sixth waves, and teacher authority also declines across the waves in which it was asked. These are the items that locate authority in wider social relations. Other items do not show the same pattern. Conflict avoidance remains widely endorsed. Fatalism is broadly stable. Filial piety rises and then returns closer to its earlier level. So the evidence does not support a story of uniform cultural decline. It points instead to selective weakening in wider social hierarchy. [Sources] - Manuscript, Cultural Change Across Six Waves - NSTC/MHH-FULL/NSTC-ABS/Figures/Figure_1_Traditionalism_Items_by_Wave.png

presenter: Brief notes: - Figure 2 translates item trends into profiles. - NNN and NNY become more common. - NYY and NYN decline. - Fully traditional YYY remains present and variable. - Recombination is the key word. The type distribution shows how item-level change alters cultural profiles. Between the first and sixth waves, the low-on-all type, NNN, becomes more common. The General-only type, NNY, also becomes more common and is the largest type in Wave 6. At the same time, the Social-General type and the Social-only type contract. That pattern closely matches the item-level decline in mother-in-law obedience and teacher authority. These are also politically relevant types, so their contraction matters for the broader argument about support. The fully traditional type does not vanish. It remains substantial and varies across waves. This is why the paper frames change as recombination. Some traditionalist profiles weaken, some persist, and some become more common. [Sources] - Manuscript, Cultural Change Across Six Waves - NSTC/MHH-FULL/NSTC-ABS/Figures/Figure_2_Traditionalism_Types_by_Wave.png

presenter: “Traditional vs. Secular-Rational Values” and “Survival vs. Self-Expression Values”, Brief notes: - Bring the model and trend evidence together. - Cultural change: Social hierarchy weakens most clearly. - Persistence: conflict avoidance, filial obligation and fatalism. - Political support: Social authority is a strong correlate. - Core-only is weaker than Social or mixed profiles. Putting the model and trend evidence together gives us the paper's main empirical story. The values that changed most clearly are not all traditionalist values. The clearest movement is away from wider social hierarchy, especially teacher authority and obedience in the extended family. At the same time, other orientations remain more persistent. Conflict avoidance is still common. Fatalism is stable. Filial obligation fluctuates but does not simply disappear. This means that Taiwan's cultural change is uneven. The political consequence follows from the typology. Social authority is one of the strongest correlates of establishment support. Harmony matters most when it is joined to Core or Social authority. Core-only traditionalism is weaker. The decline of Social Traditionalism therefore matters because it concerns a dimension that is strongly linked to support. [Sources] - Manuscript, Cultural Change Across Six Waves - Manuscript, Typology and Establishment Support

presenter: Brief notes: - Connect the item, typology, validation and trend findings. - Social Traditionalism is the strongest recurring dimension. - Core-only is weak; combinations carry the relationship. - Direct regime support has a narrower pattern. - Taiwan shows selective cultural change and recombination. The discussion brings together four pieces of evidence. First, the item-level models show that traditional values do not behave alike. Teacher authority, mother-in-law obedience and conflict avoidance are politically consequential, whereas collectivism is not a consistent predictor. Second, the typology shows why combinations matter. Social Traditionalism is the most consistent correlate of establishment support. Core Traditionalism by itself does not distinguish respondents from the low-on-all group, but it becomes consequential when combined with Social authority or General harmony. Third, the direct regime-support indicators produce a narrower pattern. The strongest repeated associations belong to YYY, NYY and YNY. Each combines conflict avoidance with at least one authority dimension. This suggests that trust in governing elites and attachment to the political system have overlapping but different cultural foundations. Finally, the six-wave trends show selective change. Social deference declines most clearly, while filial obligation, fatalism and conflict avoidance remain more persistent. Taiwan's cultural development is therefore best described as recombination within traditionalism: some configurations contract, others persist, and their political implications differ. [Sources] - Discussion and conclusion draft, "Authority, Harmony and the Changing Foundations of Regime Support" - Manuscript, Tables 2 and 4 - Manuscript, Appendix Table 5 - Manuscript, Figures 1 and 2

presenter: Brief notes: - State the final answer to the research question. - Cultural foundations changed without disappearing. - Declining social deference may make support more performance-dependent. - Keep the interpretation associational. - Finish with comparative and causal extensions. The paper's final conclusion is that Confucian and traditionalist orientations remain connected to diffuse regime support in Taiwan, but the relationship is located in particular configurations of authority and harmony. The clearest cultural change is the weakening of deference in wider social relations. Social Traditionalism is also one of the dimensions most consistently associated with establishment support. As fewer citizens accept these inherited status relations, political authorities may receive less habitual endorsement. Support may consequently depend more heavily on institutional performance, representation and current political alignments. This has particular significance for Taiwan, where democratic institutions operate amid intense domestic competition and sustained external pressure. The evidence does not show that declining social deference causes populism, third-party voting or anti-establishment mobilisation. It identifies a cultural condition under which dissatisfaction may be expressed with fewer inherited restraints. The limitations are equally important. These are observational associations. The six-wave establishment measure partly concerns governing elites, and the direct system-support indicators are available only from Wave 3 onwards. Repeated cross-sections also cannot separate individual conversion from generational replacement. The next step is comparative and causal: testing the typology across East and Southeast Asia, examining alternative measurement strategies, and using panel or experimental designs. For now, the Taiwan evidence shows that democratic development changes the cultural basis of political authority while older orientations towards hierarchy and harmony continue to shape how political institutions are judged. [Sources] - Discussion and conclusion draft, "Authority, Harmony and the Changing Foundations of Regime Support" - Manuscript, Cultural Change Across Six Waves - Manuscript, Appendix A

presenter: Brief notes: - Validation uses Waves 3-6 direct DRS items. - The first three outcomes support the typology. - Strongest repeated types: YYY, NYY and YNY. - General Traditionalism works best with Core or Social authority. - Prefer our system is the weaker validation outcome. 1. Over the long run, our system of government is capable of solving the problems our country faces. 2. Thinking in general, I am proud of our system of government. 3. A system like ours, even if it runs into problems, deserves the people’s support. The direct regime-support items provide a stricter validation test because they ask about the system of government rather than the people who run government. These items are available from Wave 3 onward, so the sample is smaller. The first three outcomes support the typological argument. Respondents in the fully traditional type, YYY, are more likely to say the system can solve problems, to express pride in the system and to say that it deserves support despite problems. Types 6 and 7, NYY and YNY, show a similar pattern. This suggests that General Traditionalism matters most when it is attached to Core or Social authority. The fourth item asks whether respondents prefer the current system over any other they can imagine. That comparative wording produces a different pattern. The typology does not consistently predict this outcome, which usefully narrows the claim: traditionalism is associated with acceptance of the existing system, but not necessarily with rejecting all possible alternatives. [Sources] - Manuscript, Table 5 - all findings_2.txt

presenter: Brief notes: - Use this slide to orient the audience to the Taiwan ABS time structure. - The analysis covers Waves 1-6, 2001-2022. - Wave 7 is shown as a next-wave reference, not analysed. - This timing is what makes the cultural-change section possible. Detailed script: Before moving to measurement, it is useful to show the survey timetable for Taiwan. The Asian Barometer timetable lists Taiwan fieldwork in Wave 1 in June-July 2001, Wave 2 in January-February 2006, Wave 3 in January-February 2010, Wave 4 in June-November 2014, Wave 5 in July 2018-January 2019, and Wave 6 in September-November 2022. Those are the six waves used in the current analysis. They cover more than two decades of Taiwan's democratic development and give the paper its pooled and over-time structure. The same Asian Barometer page also lists Taiwan for Wave 7 from 2026 onward, but that wave is a future or next-wave reference here and is not included in the empirical models. [Sources] - Asian Barometer Survey, "Survey - Timetable", Taiwan entries: https://asianbarometer.org/survey.jsp?page=s10 - Manuscript, Data, Measurement and Research Design

presenter: Brief notes: - Tie the paper back to Taiwan Data Futures. - Long-running surveys allow cultural change to be measured over time. - Harmonised repeated items support typological measurement. - The ABS makes it possible to connect political culture with legitimacy and anti-establishment sentiment. - Point to future comparative work. For this conference, the broader contribution is also about data infrastructure. The Asian Barometer Taiwan series allows us to connect long-standing debates about Confucian political culture with current questions about legitimacy, anti-establishment sentiment and democratic support. The value of repeated surveys is not only that they produce trend lines. With careful harmonisation, repeated items can support richer measurement of cultural profiles. In this paper, the six-wave structure allows us to ask which traditionalist orientations persist, which weaken, and which combinations remain politically relevant. This is especially useful in Taiwan, where democratic politics operates under changing domestic alignments and external pressure. The next step is to consider how this single-country design might travel to comparative work across East Asia and, potentially, Southeast Asia. [Sources] - NSTC/Conference_info.md - Manuscript, Abstract and Cultural Change Across Six Waves
